chunks: From him, from al-‘Abbās ibn Ma‘rūf, from al-Ḥasan ibn Maḥbūb, from some of our companions, from Abī Baṣīr, from Abī ‘Abdillāh عليه السلام, who said:
The one engaged in hunting is not subject to qaṣr for three days; then when he goes beyond the three, it becomes binding upon him.

So the proper way of reconciling these two reports is that whoever hunts for his own sustenance and the sustenance of his dependents, qaṣr is binding upon him; and whoever hunts for amusement and wantonness, qaṣr is not permissible for him, according to what we have explained. And that which indicates this is...

key_terms.الْبَطَرِ: for insolence, excess, or reckless pleasure
key_terms.عِيَالِهِ: his dependents or family members under his care
key_terms.قُوتِهِ: his sustenance or means of livelihood

ai.seo_question: Does a person traveling for hunting perform qaṣr salat (prayer), and does the ruling differ between livelihood hunting and recreational hunting?
ai.summary: This text discusses the legal ruling of qaṣr for a hunter while traveling. It distinguishes between hunting for livelihood, in which qaṣr applies, and hunting for amusement and recklessness, in which qaṣr is not permitted, showing the importance of intention and purpose in travel-related rulings.
